Carbon dating (pronounced ˈkər-bɑndɒn, from Latin carbonis, "carbon") is an age dating technique used to determine the age of an object by measuring the rate of radioactive decay of the isotope carbon-14 (14C) in the object.
The technique is based on the idea that radioactive carbon dating does not work well in organic material because the carbon atoms are too highly bonded together. This high degree of bonding makes it very difficult for the 14C to travel through the material, so it has to be incorporated into other radioactive isotopes to reach the places where it can be measured. 14CO2, which is the result of 14-carbon atoms in 14 C molecules being split, is one such isotopic species. Other radioactive species are 14O, 14N, and 14S. The technique has been applied to many samples and can provide ages of about 10,000 years or more. Carbon dating requires a technique to separate the radioactive atoms from the other carbon molecules, such as by washing the sample. Some samples may be contaminated and therefore cannot be separated by this method. Others are not contaminated, but do not have enough 14 CO2 to measure accurately. Therefore, they must be treated before the technique can begin. It can also be used with other techniques, including radiocarbon dating. In this case, the ages are calculated by comparing the amount of carbon found in carbonized remains and the abundance of radiogenic carbon in other parts of nature.

Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a disease that causes the heart to fail, usually by over-stressing the blood vessels. PH is one of the most common causes of heart failure in the United States and other developed countries.
The disease is caused by a combination of genetic and environmental factors. The main genetic risk factor is the HLA-B27 gene, which is responsible for determining how our immune system responds to certain foreign substances. When we are born, our blood cells are made from a mix of blood from our parents and blood that has been donated from another person. Our immune systems then recognize the foreign substance, called a foreign antigen, and make antibodies that attack the antigen. People with the B27-DQ2 gene have a slightly different immune response to these foreign antigens. This difference leads to a condition called polymicrogyria, where blood is produced too quickly, causing the walls of veins and arteries to thicken and become inflamed. In some cases, this condition can cause damage to the lungs.

Who wrote Second Corinthians?
Second Corinthians, by Paul, was one of the last of his letters to the Church. It was written after the death of Paul and the imprisonment of Timothy. His relationship with Timothy was more like brother than father, but the two had a strong bond. They were both the sons of God. In this letter, Paul talks about the Christian life, his own life and his relationship to Timothy, who is now in prison. He also refers to himself in the third person as ‘I’.
There are four main sections in this book:
The first section of this work is a letter to a man by the name of Philemon. Philetus was a Christian who had been Paul's disciple. When Paul was in Corinth, Philitus went away to live in Rome. This letter is to him. After Paul has finished his letter Philipeus sends it to Paul to be read. At the end of it, he asks Paul if he would like to write a second letter. But Paul is not at all sure he wants to. However, at the suggestion of a friend, Philip, a Jew, they get a scribe to copy the letter and send it on to Phyllis. Philip writes the second part of an apologetic letter for Paul. Then, after Paul reads the first letter he writes a third letter back. Finally, when he is at Corinth he sends the whole letter on again. So, two letters have been written by him to this man and one has been sent on. If this is the case, how did Paul know what to say in both letters? Did he have the ability to send a reply to someone who he had never met before? Or did he write to people who knew him very well? It is possible that he was writing to two different groups of people. A man he knew very little about, or a close friend.
